counterexample: Take A = [1, 2, 5] (sorted non-decreasing), t = 6, l = 0, r = 1. Every hypothesis of step 0010 holds: l < r (0 < 1), A[l] + A[r] = 1 + 2 = 3 < 6 = t. And the index the step assumes 'for contradiction' genuinely exists: r' = 2 > r = 1 with A[l] + A[r'] = 1 + 5 = 6 = t. So the assumption of step 0010 is satisfiable under its own stated hypotheses, and therefore no contradiction can ever be derived from it -- the proof-by-contradiction strategy is unfalsifiable as set up. Step 0012's consequence is likewise consistent here: A[r] = 2 < A[r'] = 5, which is exactly what non-decreasing sortedness with r' > r permits, so it is not the seed of any contradiction. (The state l=0, r=1 is unreachable for this input in the actual algorithm, since right starts at 2 and only moves left when the sum exceeds t; that is precisely the missing ingredient -- the loop invariant -- which step 0010 never assumes.)
reasoning_summary: Lines 0001-0009 are problem statement and narration; the mathematical argument begins at 0010. Step 0010 sets up a proof by contradiction from only three hypotheses: A is sorted non-decreasing, l < r, and A[l] + A[r] < t, then assumes some r' > r has A[l] + A[r'] = t and announces the goal of disproving that r'. This step fails: under those hypotheses alone such an r' can exist (witness above), so the negation is not refutable and the chosen proof obligation is the wrong one. Two distinct defects sit here. (i) Missing invariant: refuting a solution at an index r' > r requires the algorithm's loop invariant -- that every pair (i, j) with i < j and A[i] + A[j] = t satisfies l <= i and j <= r, i.e. that indices already passed by the right pointer were safely eliminated -- which 0010 does not assume and which is exactly what carries the argument. (ii) Wrong obligation: advancing left when A[l] + A[r] < t discards the pairs (l, j) for l < j <= r, so what must be shown is that no j in (l, r] satisfies A[l] + A[j] = t; that follows in one line from A[j] <= A[r], giving A[l] + A[j] <= A[l] + A[r] < t. Indices beyond r are irrelevant to this move (and the right pointer is never incremented by the algorithm at all, so line 0007's framing is confused). Step 0012's inference A[r] < A[r'] is arithmetically valid but vacuous, since sortedness already implies A[r] <= A[r'] for r' > r; the proof then stops with the author stating he does not know how to continue, and no contradiction, and hence no correctness claim, is established. Early stop at 0010.
